result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.is_matching()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Check if a set of edges forms a valid matching. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L53297-L53383){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.is_matching(edges) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Is matching](/assets/graphs/is-matching.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="The same two-by-three ladder on both sides, with the candidate edges in the accent color. Left: A-D, B-C, and E-F touch six different nodes, so is_matching() returns True. Right: B-C and C-F both end at C (filled in the accent color), so is_matching() returns False." width="100%"} A matching is a set of edges where no two edges share a common endpoint (node). In other words, each node is "used" by at most one selected edge. Matchings model one-to-one pairings: workers to tasks, students to projects, donors to recipients, or any situation where each item can be paired with at most one partner. This method validates a candidate set of edges, which is useful for: - checking a hand-built or externally computed pairing before acting on it - sanity-checking the output of `maximal_matching()` or similar algorithms - enforcing a "no shared endpoints" constraint while building a pairing incrementally The check visits the edges in order and returns `False` as soon as an edge touches a node already used by an earlier edge. Edge direction is ignored (`A -> B` uses both `A` and `B`). Listing the same edge ID twice counts as a conflict, and an empty list is a valid (empty) matching. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [edges]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[Union[int, str]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A list of integer edge IDs to check, such as values from `get_edge_ids()` or the output of `maximal_matching()`. Edge labels and other strings are not accepted. If any ID does not correspond to an edge in the graph, the method returns `False`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : `True` if the edges exist and form a valid matching (no shared endpoints), `False` otherwise. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Two disjoint edges (`A-B` and `C-D`) share no endpoints, so together they form a valid matching: ::: {#bdf79492 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("C", "D")]) ) edge_ids = graph.get_edge_ids() # Returns True (no shared endpoints) graph.is_matching(edge_ids) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` True ``` ::: ::: In a path `A-B-C`, the two edges share node `B`, so they don't form a valid matching: ::: {#9e366dd5 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C")]) ) edge_ids = graph.get_edge_ids() # Returns False (B is shared) graph.is_matching(edge_ids) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` False ``` ::: ::: This makes it easy to sanity-check the output of matching algorithms like `maximal_matching()`: ::: {#a4b2a547 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_path_graph(6) matching = graph.maximal_matching() # Returns True: maximal_matching() always produces a valid matching graph.is_matching(matching) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` True ``` ::: :::
